1.pericope_label: The basket of firstfruits brought to the sanctuary and set down before the altar

schools.summary: Distinguish this private basket from the sheaf offered for the whole land after the passover, and describe the practice of going into the field as the fruits ripened, marking what was most forward, and laying by wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives and dates in one basket with leaves between them; then draw three lessons — to acknowledge God as the giver of what supports natural life, to deny ourselves, since what is first ripe is what we are fondest of and laying it by teaches us to prefer his name to our appetite, and to give God the first and best as those who believe him the first and best of beings, which is what those do who consecrate the days of their youth.

Explain that the firstfruits were required for the same reason as the tribute for every soul, that they might confess themselves and all they had to be God's, but with this difference, that where the tribute symbolised their emancipation the firstfruits testified that the land was tributary and they held it only as tenants at will, the sovereignty remaining with God; so that the rite renewed yearly the recollection of their adoption, they being fed not promiscuously like the Gentiles but like children, their food therefore sacred; add that the typical rite has ceased while its true observation remains, since whether we eat or drink we are to do all to the glory of God, and that the words the offerer says confess the land was gained neither by strength nor by fortune but by free gift according to promise, dating themselves from Jacob rather than Abraham because in him grace shone out more brightly. Elsewhere separate this offering from the barley sheaf, the two wave loaves and the cake of the dough, note that only seven kinds were owed, report that the priest waved the basket with his hand under the owner's toward the corners of the earth in acknowledgment that the Lord owns the whole, and pass on the reading that the priest of those days means the high priest, whom you take as typical of Christ, by whom we offer the sacrifice of praise.

Handle the one grammatical point bearing on quantity: the word is partitive, a portion of the first of the fruit, from which it does not follow — against the commentator who so argues — that the firstfruits were not all delivered at the sanctuary, but only that not all of them had to be put in a basket and set down there.

Make the offering the duty of each master of a family, either on first settling in the land or once a year at one of the three feasts; and explain its purpose as keeping them in continual remembrance of God's kindness in preserving them and fulfilling his promises, the firstfruits being consecrated to the author of every good and perfect gift.

debates: How this basket of firstfruits differed from the other firstfruit offerings of the calendar.
Whether all the firstfruits had to be delivered at the sanctuary.
When and how often the basket was to be brought.
What the offering was meant to confess about the tenure of the land.
outliers: Calvin alone pairs the firstfruits with the poll tribute and makes them opposite symbols, of tenancy and of emancipation.
Keil alone reads the partitive strictly and corrects an inference drawn from it.
Henry alone finds self-denial in the law, on the ground that the earliest fruit is the most desired.
Gill alone reports the waving of the basket toward the corners of the earth.
Calvin alone notices that the confession begins with Jacob rather than Abraham.

5.pericope_label: The confession beginning a Syrian ready to perish was my father, and the command to rejoice

schools.summary: Lay out the six ways the opening words of the confession have been rendered — that a Syrian persecuted my father, that my father abandoned Syria, that Laban endeavoured to destroy him, that he was led out of Syria into Egypt, that Laban almost destroyed him, and that famine oppressed him so that he went down into Egypt, this last got by detaching a letter and finding the sense of famine in the Arabic cognate — and judge that the Syrian is Jacob, so called from his long residence with his father-in-law, his being ready to perish referring to the hard usage and severe labour of that service; take the epithet as true also by origin, since the patriarchs came from Mesopotamia, by education and conversation, and by his wives and children, and leave the peril open between poverty and the rage of a brother and the treachery of a father-in-law; and press the command to rejoice, since God intends his followers to be happy and to eat their bread with gladness and singleness of heart, while those who eat grudgingly under pretence of unworthiness profane his bounties and get no thanks for their voluntary humility — the Levite having no inheritance and the stranger no home, let the one rejoice with you and the other find you his friend and father, and let a man take comfort in all his employments once he has sanctified them by giving God his portion, tracing the streams up to the fountain.

Render the opening of the confession as a lost, a perishing Aramaean was my father, against the versions that make the Aramaean Laban the one who sought to destroy him; reject the reading by which the renewed command to set the basket down implies that the offerer held it in his hand throughout the prayer, in direct opposition to the earlier verses, treating the words instead as a remark closing the instructions; and hold that the rejoicing points to the sacrificial meal following the act of worship, and that the presentation was made on the pilgrimages to the sanctuary at the three yearly festivals, against the attempt to restrict the words to meals prepared from the tithes.

Note that the offerer was to lift up his voice, or, on another reading, to answer the priest's question what is this thou hast brought; that the evil entreatment was the two edicts, first that the midwives should kill the male children and then that the people should drown them; that the bringing to this place came only after forty years' travel through the wilderness; and that the good things to rejoice in are all the blessings of goodness and mercies of life which God in his kind providence had bestowed.

debates: How the opening words of the confession should be rendered, and whether the Syrian is Jacob or Laban.
In what sense Jacob was ready to perish.
Whether the renewed command to set down the basket means the offerer held it throughout the prayer.
What occasion the rejoicing belongs to, and who is to share in it.
outliers: Clarke assembles six competing renderings of the same four words before giving his own.
Wesley alone makes the epithet true on three separate grounds at once.
Keil alone treats the repetition at verse 10 as a closing remark rather than a description of the offerer's posture.
Clarke alone warns that grudging use of God's gifts under a show of unworthiness is itself a profanation.

12.pericope_label: The third year's tithe, the protestation that it was rightly disposed of, and the prayer for blessing

schools.summary: Explain that the second tithe, spent in the other two years on extraordinaries at the feasts, was in the third year spent at home in entertaining the poor; hold that because it was disposed of out of sight of the priests, and great confidence was reposed in the people's honesty, the protestation was made at the sanctuary at the next feast, as it were upon oath, that the trust had been faithfully kept; and draw the parallel that though we are no longer under such appropriations of our revenue we are commanded to give alms, and then, and not otherwise, all things are clean to us — noting that the clause about forgetting forecloses the excuse that the commandment slipped the mind.

Describe how the third year widened the company from owners and Levites at Jerusalem to strangers, fatherless and widows in their own dwellings, and note that by the letter of the law the tithe was for the Levites and drawn only once in three years; call the declaration a private address to God, said solemnly but at home; take eating in mourning to mean grudging rather than grief — not eaten in sorrow at giving away so much of one's profits, but cheerfully feasted with the poor as commanded; read the giving to the dead as funeral feasting, since provisions were sent to the relations of the deceased and both guests and food were then legally polluted, a double fault, while elsewhere reading it of idolatry, an idol being generally a dead man whom ignorance had deified, and comparing the flesh offered to idols and afterwards sold in the shambles; and take the order of profession and prayer as instruction in how vain the prayers of disobedient persons are.

Report the rabbinic ruling that the tithing was reckoned finished at the passover, and deny that the declaration was made in the tabernacle or temple at all, since the tithe was eaten in the owner's own gates; observe that Moses stimulates them by setting God before their eyes as if the tithes were paid into his hand, nothing awakening men more than when God is produced as their judge, so that the speaker condemns himself if he has defrauded and prays for grace if he has not; insist that the claim not to have transgressed or forgotten refers to the matter in hand only, since it would be temerity and arrogance to boast of having kept the whole law, the words signifying desire rather than perfection; canvass three renderings of the second denial and prefer the adverbial sense, that nothing was appropriated impurely; follow the funeral reading of the third while objecting that it is unclear why such a denial should be needed; take eating in mourning, with almost universal consent, to mean that even poverty did not tempt them to touch the hallowed things, while allowing that it might mean the anxiety of a guilty mind; conclude from the command to bless a land already flowing with milk and honey that it was not fertile by nature but because God daily watered it by his secret blessing; and read the petition as asking God to look with an eye of complacency from heaven on people unholy in themselves.

State flatly that saying before the Lord here does not denote prayer in the sanctuary, and explain why a prayer is prescribed for this tithe and not the others — because this one was consumed throughout the land in meals for the poor, so that the requirement would not follow by analogy from the firstfruits, as it would where the meal was eaten at the sanctuary; and take eating in mourning to mean mourning for the dead, that is, a state of legal uncleanness, the second denial meaning that nothing was removed while in that state.

debates: What changed about the tithe in the third year, and who ate it.
Whether the protestation was made at the sanctuary or at home.
How a man could claim not to have transgressed or forgotten the commandments.
What eating in mourning means, and what giving to the dead means.
Why a land already flowing with milk and honey should need to be blessed.
outliers: Henry alone places the protestation at the sanctuary; three others place it at home.
Keil alone explains why this tithe and no other required a prayer.
Calvin alone defuses the apparent claim to perfect obedience by reading it as desire rather than achievement.
Wesley alone takes mourning to mean grudging the gift rather than grieving for the dead.
Calvin alone infers from the prayer that the fertility of Canaan was maintained daily rather than native to it.

16.pericope_label: The mutual avouching, and the promise to set Israel high above all nations

schools.summary: Take this day as Moses' own word, covering everything repeated in the book, since this was the last day on which the whole account was finished, and add the rabbinic turn that every day was to be reckoned new, as if the laws had been given that morning; note that the exaltation is comparative — other nations were made famous for extent, wealth and number, but Israel stood higher for having the Lord as God and King and for having such laws, the end being to make them not merely high but holy; leave the verse at one point for a paragraph on the elect in Christ among all nations, adopted, regenerated and certified by the Spirit; insist that God is the author of the Law and that men grow careless unless often stirred up, so that by often calling them to obedience God indirectly rebukes their indifference; explain with all thy soul as serious apprehension free of disguise, nothing being more displeasing to God than hypocrisy; answer the objection that no mortal can keep the Law with the whole heart by saying that the whole heart is set against a divided one and means an undeceitful one, and that it is not absurd to propose to believers an object they aim at though the flesh keeps them from reaching it; and make the exaltation reciprocal but hidden, since God desires to be glorified only by making us partakers of his glory, while this excellency of the Church, being spiritual, obtains its praise before God and the angels alone.

Draw two enforcements from the passage. First, that these are God's commands and not the dictates of the lawgiver's own wisdom — do them and not dispute them, do them and not draw back, and not carelessly or hypocritically but with the whole heart and soul. Second, that the covenant binds both ways: Israel had avouched God implicitly by attending on his word and expressly at Sinai, and would do so again before parting, from which it follows that we forswear ourselves and violate the most sacred engagement if, having taken the Lord for our God, we do not make conscience of obeying him.

Find two things in the mutual avouching: that Israel's acceptance of the laws was a practical declaration that the nation would take Jehovah as its God and walk in his ways, and that the Lord's giving of them was a practical confirmation of his promise that Israel should be his treasured people of possession; render the verb causatively, so that Israel did not avouch but let the Lord say it, giving him occasion to say he would be their God; and turn the three words of the promise about, so that Israel becomes an object of praise and renown and glorification, not of itself but of the God who made it, among all nations — the sanctifying of the people being the design and end of its election.

Keep the plain sense of the verb as a public declaration, and hold that God avouched on his side by the blessings he pours down and by eminent manifestations of his power and favour, so that the covenant is thereby made and ratified; then take the promised exaltation into public and national politics, since righteousness exalteth a nation but sin is a reproach to any people — Israel being the greatest of nations while it kept the testimonies and the most contemptible when it forsook them — and address your own country directly, that neither fleets nor armies, however well appointed, can secure permanence among the nations, but righteousness alone; and close on the confession itself as affecting, since men brought into affluence were commanded to remember and publicly acknowledge their former wretchedness, one who rises from poverty and forgets it becoming proud, insolent and oppressive.

debates: What this day covers, given that the laws had been rehearsed over several days.
Whether the verb means that Israel avouched God or that Israel gave God occasion to speak.
How obedience with the whole heart can be demanded if no one can render it.
What being set high above all nations consists in, and whether it is visible.
outliers: Keil alone reads the verb causatively, against the plain sense the other three keep.
Calvin twice in this chapter defuses an apparent claim of perfect obedience by distinguishing the aim from the attainment.
Calvin makes the exaltation spiritual and hidden from the world; Clarke makes it national and visible, and applies it to his own country by name.
Gill turns the avouching into a paragraph on the elect in Christ, well beyond the verse.
Clarke alone ends the chapter by reflecting on what remembering former poverty does to a man who has grown rich.
